readerTitle: Google's first two checks: why angels and venture capital want different things
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Google의 1998년 엔젤 투자와 1999년 VC 투자) + 가상 적용 (라멘 가게, 치과용 예약 소프트웨어, 펀드 계산)
insight: 투자자를 고를 때는 수표 크기보다 '누구의 돈이고, 그 돈의 주인이 무엇을 돌려받아야 하는가'를 먼저 본다.
misconception: 좋은 사업이면 VC가 투자한다. 가장 큰 금액을 주는 투자자가 가장 좋은 투자자다.

sources.text: Google, 'Our history' / 'From the garage to the Googleplex' (Bechtolsheim의 $100,000 수표, 1998년 9월 법인 설립)
Google press release, June 7, 1999: Google receives $25 million in equity funding from Sequoia Capital and Kleiner Perkins Caufield & Byers (Michael Moritz, John Doerr 이사회 합류)
VC 펀드 구조(LP, 약 10년 펀드 기간)와 멱법칙 수익 분포는 벤처 금융의 일반적 설명. 펀드 계산은 설명용 가상 수치

factChecks.note: Bechtolsheim 수표: 1998년 8월, 'Google Inc.' 앞으로 $100,000, 법인이 아직 없어 몇 주간 현금화하지 못함. Google 공식 역사 자료로 게시 직전 재확인하세요. 데모를 본 뒤 바로 결정했다는 세부 묘사는 카드에 넣지 않았습니다.
1999년 6월 Sequoia Capital과 Kleiner Perkins의 $25 million 투자, 두 파트너의 이사회 합류는 Google 1999년 보도자료 기준입니다. 재확인 필요.
펀드 계산(가상): $100M 펀드, 한 건 $5M 투자로 지분 10%. 10% × $1B = $100M = 펀드 전체 금액. $20M 회사의 10%는 $2M로 펀드의 2%에 불과.
'약 10년' 펀드 기간은 일반적 관행이며 펀드마다 연장 조항 등으로 다릅니다. 카드에는 'usually within about ten years'로 적었습니다. 특정 국가의 투자·법률 조언은 다루지 않습니다.

cards.title: A $100,000 check to a company that didn't exist yet
body: In August 1998, Andy Bechtolsheim, a co-founder of Sun Microsystems, wrote a $100,000 check to "Google Inc." The company hadn't been legally formed, so the founders couldn't cash it for weeks.
Ten months later, two venture capital firms put in $25 million. Same company, two very different kinds of money.

image.label: A small personal check next to a large stack of fund money
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에 손으로 쓴 작은 개인 수표 한 장, 오른쪽에 'Fund'라고 적힌 커다란 금고와 돈다발. 둘 사이에 작은 차고 모양 건물. 실제 기업 로고나 서명은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You need $400,000 for a third ramen shop.
body: You own two busy ramen shops. Both earn a steady profit. You need $400,000 to open a third shop and a small central kitchen.
A friend says venture capital firms have the deepest pockets. Who do you approach first?

options.text: Venture capital firms, since they write the biggest checks
options.feedback: Most will pass, not because the shops are bad, but because three shops can't become the size of outcome their funds need. You may lose months chasing the wrong money.

options.text: A few local angels: regulars and business owners who know the shops
options.feedback: Their money fits your plan: modest size, patient, and happy with a good return rather than a giant one. You still need clear written terms.

options.text: Skip investors and get a bank loan
options.feedback: A fair option for a proven, cash-producing business, and you keep ownership. But it adds fixed repayments every month, good months or bad.

cards.title: Two checks, two different bets.
body: Bechtolsheim was investing his own money. He could decide on his own judgment, and he answered to nobody if it went to zero.
Sequoia Capital and Kleiner Perkins were investing from their funds. Their $25 million came with two board seats and a clear expectation: Google had to become very large.
Both bets paid off. But they were made for different reasons, by people with different needs.

cards.title: Angels vs venture capital
body: An **angel** is a person investing their own money, usually early and in smaller amounts.

A **venture capital (VC) firm** invests other people's money. Pension funds, university endowments and wealthy families put money into a fund. The firm must return it with a profit, usually within about ten years.
The real difference isn't check size. It's *whose* money it is, and what that owner needs back.

image.label: One person with a wallet vs a firm passing money from many owners
image.brief: 좌우 비교 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 'Angel': 한 사람이 자기 지갑에서 창업자에게 직접 돈을 건넴. 오른쪽 'VC': 여러 기관(연금, 대학, 가문) 아이콘에서 화살표가 'Fund'로 모이고, 펀드에서 창업자로, 다시 기관으로 돌아가는 화살표와 '~10 years' 시계 표시.

cards.title: Why a VC needs giants
body: Most startups a fund backs fail or return little. So a VC looks for deals where one win could repay the entire fund.

breakdown.label: Fund size
breakdown.detail: Money the firm must return, plus profit

cards.callout: A healthy company worth $20 million gives that fund just $2 million. To an angel, the same result can be excellent.

cards.title: A good business is not the same as a VC business.
body: This is why most restaurants, agencies and local service firms never raise VC, even when profitable. A VC's question isn't "Is this good?" It's "Could this become huge?"

Angels can say yes to more kinds of businesses. They can accept slower growth, a smaller sale, or a share of profits. Many bring experience too: a former restaurant owner may be worth more than the cash.
The reverse holds as well. A company chasing a global market may need more money than angels can provide.

cards.title: Each kind of money has a price.
body: Angels have limits. Most can't fund your next round, and money from friends or regulars can strain relationships if things go badly.
VC money comes with pressure to grow fast and a board that may prefer a big swing over a safe, steady business.
The labels also blur. Angel groups and small VC funds sit in between. So ask every investor directly: what return do you need, and by when?

cards.title: Now it's software for dental clinics.
body: You built scheduling software for dental clinics. Revenue grows 5% a month and you're close to breaking even. You want to stay focused on dentists. Your honest estimate: the market tops out around $20 million in yearly sales.
You need $500,000 to hire two engineers. What do you do?

options.text: Raise a VC seed round and promise to expand into all of healthcare
options.feedback: You might get the money, but you'd sign up for a plan you don't want. The fund's need for a giant outcome would start steering your product.

options.text: Raise from a few angels, ideally people who know dental practices
options.feedback: The amount, the pace and the likely outcome all match what these investors can live with. You give up the option of a fast, massive round.

options.text: Take angel money now and plan to raise VC later
options.feedback: Keeping options open is sensible, but a later VC will still need a giant outcome. If you stay dental-only, that round may never come.

cards.title: Match the investor's needs to your honest plan.
body: Angels bet their own money and can be happy with a good business. VCs bet a fund's money and need a giant one.
**Try it today:** write down the biggest realistic outcome for your business in ten years. Could 10% of it repay a $100 million fund? If not, start your list with angels.
